title: Nuclear power for Australia

draft.title: Nuclear power for Australia
card: Nuclear power stations use fission to heat water into steam, which turns turbines. Running one produces very little carbon dioxide, and it can supply steady power day and night.
Nuclear plants are expensive and take many years to build. Australia has no nuclear power stations, so it would also need new laws, skills and regulators.
Used fuel stays dangerously radioactive for a very long time and needs safe long-term storage. Rare accidents can release radioactive material and harm people and the environment.
Physics can give facts about costs, risks and benefits. Deciding whether Australia should build nuclear power also involves values, such as how much risk people accept.
draft.remember: Nuclear power gives steady, low-carbon electricity, but it has high costs and waste and safety risks to weigh.

a.q: Which is a benefit of nuclear power compared with a coal power station?
opts: It produces very little carbon dioxide while running
It is cheap and quick to build in a new country
It produces no radioactive waste at all
It cannot be affected by any accident
a.why: Fission heats water without burning fuel, so running the plant gives off very little carbon dioxide. The other options are wrong because nuclear plants are costly and slow to build, and they make used fuel that stays radioactive.
a.clue: Think about what is burnt in a coal station and what is not burnt here.

b.q: A Victorian council argues that Australia should build a nuclear plant because it is the right thing to do. Which part of this argument rests on a value judgement rather than physics?
opts: That building it is the right thing to do
That fission releases energy to heat water
That used fuel stays radioactive for a long time
That a plant can supply steady power day and night
b.why: Whether something is the right thing to do depends on what people value, such as how much risk they accept. The other three are facts about how nuclear plants work, and they can be tested with evidence.
b.clue: Which statement could not be settled by measurement alone?

a.best: It produces very little carbon dioxide while running

b.best: That building it is the right thing to do

problems.detail: The stem states the argument rests on 'the right thing to do', and only the right option repeats that phrase. The other three options are not part of the council's argument as described, so a student can match words without understanding value judgements versus physics facts. Better: describe an argument that mixes several factual claims with one value claim.

The right option is the only one with a hedged qualifier ('very little', 'while running'). Two distractors are obvious absolutes ('cannot be affected by any accident', 'no radioactive waste at all'), so test-wise students can pick it without knowing the idea.

check.summary: The card's facts are accurate and both intended answers are correct. Question b gives its answer away by repeating the stem's 'right thing to do' wording, and in question a the right option stands out against absolute-worded distractors.

proposal.title: Nuclear power for Australia
card: Nuclear power stations use fission to heat water into steam, which turns turbines. Running one produces very little carbon dioxide, and it can supply steady power day and night.
Nuclear plants are expensive and take many years to build. Australia has no nuclear power stations, so it would also need new laws, skills and regulators.
Used fuel stays dangerously radioactive for a very long time and needs safe long-term storage. Rare accidents can release radioactive material and harm people and the environment.
Physics can give facts about costs, risks and benefits. Deciding whether Australia should build nuclear power also involves values, such as how much risk people accept.
proposal.remember: Nuclear power gives steady, low-carbon electricity, but it has high costs and waste and safety risks to weigh.

a.q: Which is a benefit of nuclear power compared with a coal power station?
opts: It gives off much less carbon dioxide while making power
It costs much less to build than a coal station of equal size
Its used fuel becomes safe after a few years in storage
It can be built faster than most other power stations
a.why: Fission heats water without burning fuel, so a running plant gives off far less carbon dioxide than coal. Nuclear plants are expensive and slow to build, and their used fuel stays radioactive for a very long time, so the other options are wrong.
a.clue: Think about what a coal station burns that a nuclear plant does not.

b.q: A Victorian council report argues for a nuclear plant. Which of its claims is a value judgement rather than a physics fact?
opts: The small chance of an accident is a risk worth accepting
The plant would supply steady power day and night
The plant would release little carbon dioxide while running
The used fuel would need storing for a very long time
b.why: Whether a risk is worth accepting depends on what people value, so evidence alone cannot settle it. The claim about storing used fuel may sound like an opinion, but how long fuel stays radioactive can be measured, just like the claims about steady power and carbon dioxide.
b.clue: Which claim could not be settled by measurement alone?
